08.01.title: The harmonic oscillator
08.01.html:
Pluck a guitar string, tap a wine glass, hit a bronze key of a Balinese gamelan or drive a car over a speed bump. Each one rings at its own frequency. Almost every vibration problem in engineering starts from one model: a mass on a spring.

Equation of motion

A mass m sits on a spring of stiffness k. Measure x from the static equilibrium position, so gravity is already balanced by the spring’s preload and drops out. Displace the mass and the spring pushes back with −kx. Newton’s second law gives

mx¨+kx=0.

Try x=Acos(ωt)+Bsin(ωt). Substituting gives (k−mω2)x=0, so motion is possible only at

ωn​=mk​​,fn​=2πωn​​,T=2πkm​​.

A and B come from the start: A=x0​ and B=v0​/ωn​.

What the formula says

  • Stiffer means higher frequency; heavier means lower, both as square roots. Doubling the mass lengthens the period by 2​.
  • The frequency doesn’t depend on the amplitude. A linear spring gives the same period for small and large swings, which is why a tuning fork holds its pitch as it fades.
  • Energy swaps between the spring and the mass: 21​mx˙2+21​kx2 stays constant.

The static-deflection shortcut

Under gravity the spring sags by δ=mg/k. So k/m=g/δ and

fn​=2π1​δg​​.

Measure how much something sags and you know its natural frequency without weighing it. A sag of 25 mm gives about 3.2 Hz; 250 mm gives 1 Hz.

Worked exampleA quarter of a car

One corner of a car carries m=300 kg on a spring of k=30 kN/m (ignore the damper for now).

  1. ωn​=30000/300​=10.000 rad/s, so fn​=1.5915 Hz and T=0.6283 s.
  2. Simulating 10 s with velocity Verlet at Δt=1 ms and measuring zero crossings gives 0.628316 s against 2πm/k​=0.628319 s.
  3. Released from 50 mm the energy is 37.5 J, conserved to 2.5×10−5. Releasing from 1 mm or 200 mm gives the same period.
  4. Static sag 300⋅9.81/30000=98.1 mm, and 9.81/0.0981​/2π=1.5915 Hz, the same answer.
  5. Doubling the mass to 600 kg gives a period of 0.8886 s, a ratio of 1.4142.

Car suspensions are tuned to about 1 to 1.5 Hz, close to the rhythm of walking, which people find comfortable.

Exercise 1A gamelan key

A bronze gamelan key rings at 440 Hz. Treat its first mode as a mass-spring with an effective mass of 0.12 kg. What effective stiffness does that imply? If the maker grinds the key so its effective mass drops by 4 % with the same stiffness, what is the new pitch?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. k=mωn2​=0.12⋅(2π⋅440)2=9.17×105 N/m.
  2. f∝1/m​, so f=440/0.96​=449.1 Hz.
  3. Real tuning is subtler: grinding the middle of a bar reduces its stiffness more than its mass and lowers the pitch, while grinding the ends raises it.

quiz.q: Natural frequency (Hz) of 300 kg on a 30 kN/m spring. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: fn​=k/m​/2π.

quiz.q: Natural frequency (Hz) of a machine that sags 25 mm on its mounts. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: fn​=g/δ​/2π.

quiz.q: Effective stiffness (N/m) of the 440 Hz key with 0.12 kg effective mass. 3 significant figures.
quiz.explain: k=mωn2​.

quiz.q: Doubling the amplitude of a linear oscillator changes its period by…
quiz.explain: The period is independent of amplitude.

quiz.q: To halve a natural frequency at fixed mass you must…
quiz.explain: f∝k​.

08.02.title: Damping
08.02.html:
A real oscillator dies away. Friction in joints, air drag, internal friction in rubber and steel, and purpose-built shock absorbers all turn vibration energy into heat. The simplest model that captures this, and the one engineers use almost everywhere, is a viscous damper: a force proportional to velocity.

The damped equation

Add a damper of coefficient c (N s/m):

mx¨+cx˙+kx=0.

Divide by m and write it with two numbers that describe any such system, the natural frequency ωn​=k/m​ and the damping ratio

ζ=2km​c​,x¨+2ζωn​x˙+ωn2​x=0.

Trying x=est gives s=−ζωn​±ωn​ζ2−1​. Three cases follow.

  • Underdamped, ζ<1: it oscillates at the damped frequency ωd​=ωn​1−ζ2​ inside an envelope e−ζωn​t. Almost all structures and machines are here, typically with ζ from 0.005 (a steel bridge) to 0.3 (a car suspension).
  • Critically damped, ζ=1: the fastest return to rest without overshoot. Door closers and gauge needles aim for this.
  • Overdamped, ζ>1: no oscillation, and a slower creep back.

Logarithmic decrement

You can’t easily measure c directly, but you can record a decaying vibration. Successive peaks one damped period apart shrink by a constant factor. The logarithmic decrement is

δ=lnxi+1​xi​​=1−ζ2​2πζ​,ζ=4π2+δ2​δ​.

For light damping, measure over n cycles and use δ=n1​ln(xi​/xi+n​). With noisy data, fitting a straight line through lnxi​ against cycle number uses every peak and is better still.

Worked exampleFinding ζ from a recording

Quarter-car: m=300 kg, k=30 kN/m, damper c=1200 N s/m, released from 50 mm.

  1. ζ=1200/(230000⋅300​)=0.200; ωd​=101−0.04​=9.798 rad/s.
  2. Simulated peaks (refined with a parabola through three samples): 13.87, 3.85, 1.07, 0.30 mm. Each is 0.2773 times the previous.
  3. δ=ln(1/0.2773)=1.2825, so ζ=1.2825/4π2+1.28252​=0.2000. The test asked for 2 %; it hits it exactly.
  4. A lightly damped structure with ζ=0.01: both one-cycle and ten-cycle estimates give 0.01000 from clean data. Add 0.5 mm of random noise and the one-cycle estimate drifts to 0.0098, while a straight-line fit over 29 cycles still returns 0.0100.

Exercise 1A footbridge test

Engineers jump on a footbridge and record its decay. The peak acceleration falls from 0.80 m/s² to 0.35 m/s² over 12 cycles at 2.1 Hz. Estimate ζ. How long does it take to fall to 5 % of its starting level?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. δ=121​ln(0.80/0.35)=0.06889.
  2. ζ=0.06889/4π2+0.068892​=0.01096, about 1.1 %, typical of a steel footbridge.
  3. The amplitude falls by e−δ per cycle: n=ln20/δ=43.5 cycles, which is 20.7 s at 2.1 Hz.

quiz.q: Damping ratio of m = 300 kg, k = 30 kN/m, c = 1200 N s/m. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: c/(2km​).
2πζ/1−ζ2​.

quiz.q: Damping ratio of the footbridge (0.80 to 0.35 m/s² in 12 cycles). 5 decimals.
quiz.explain: δ=n1​ln(x0​/xn​).

quiz.q: For light damping, why measure the decrement over many cycles?
quiz.explain: Many cycles give a large, well-measured ratio.

08.03.title: Forced vibration and resonance
08.03.html:
Push a child on a swing at the right moment and small pushes build a big swing. Machines do the same to whatever they sit on: an unbalanced pump on a floor, an engine in a car body, a crowd on a grandstand. When the forcing frequency nears a natural frequency, the response can be many times larger than the static deflection. That’s resonance.

Steady-state response

Drive the damped oscillator with a harmonic force F0​cosωt:

mx¨+cx˙+kx=F0​cosωt.

After the start-up transient decays, the mass moves at the forcing frequency with amplitude X and a phase lag φ. Using complex notation, F=F0​eiωt and x=Xei(ωt−φ), the frequency response (receptance) is

H(ω)=F0​Xe−iφ​=k−mω2+icω1​.

With the frequency ratio r=ω/ωn​:

F0​/kX​=(1−r2)2+(2ζr)2​1​,tanφ=1−r22ζr​.

Three regions

  • Well below resonance (r≪1): the spring dominates. X≈F0​/k, in phase with the force.
  • At resonance (r=1): spring and inertia cancel and only damping limits the motion. X=(F0​/k)/(2ζ), lagging the force by 90°. That 90° lag is the cleanest way to spot a resonance in a test.
  • Well above resonance (r≫1): inertia dominates. X≈F0​/(mω2), falling fast, and 180° out of phase.

The amplitude peaks slightly below ωn​, at ωn​1−2ζ2​, with height 1/(2ζ1−ζ2​). For ζ>0.707 there is no peak at all.

Worked exampleA machine on rubber mounts

m=200 kg, k=2×105 N/m, ζ=0.05, driven by F0​=500 N.

  1. ωn​=31.623 rad/s (5.033 Hz); c=2ζkm​=632.5 N s/m; static deflection F0​/k=2.50 mm.
  2. Searching ∣H∣ on a fine grid puts the peak at 31.544 rad/s, matching ωn​1−2ζ2​=31.544.
  3. Peak amplitude 25.031 mm, an amplification of 10.0125, matching 1/(2ζ1−ζ2​).
  4. Integrating the forced equation for 60 cycles with RK4 and measuring the last 5:
r ∣H∣F0​ (mm) simulated (mm) phase lag
0.5 3.3260 3.3259 3.81°
1.0 25.0000 25.0000 90.00°
2.0 0.8315 0.8315 176.19°

Exercise 1Staying clear of resonance

A 50 kg fan unit on springs with ζ=0.03 runs at 1450 rpm. Its rotor produces a 40 N force at running speed. The springs give a natural frequency of 20 Hz. Find the amplitude at running speed, and what it would be if the springs were swapped for ones giving 24 Hz.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ω=1450⋅2π/60=151.8 rad/s, which is 24.17 Hz.
  2. With fn​=20 Hz: k=50(2π⋅20)2=7.896×105 N/m, r=1.208, amplification 1/(1−1.460)2+(0.0725)2​=2.147. X=2.147⋅40/7.896×105=0.109 mm.
  3. With fn​=24 Hz: r=1.007, amplification 16.1, and X=0.57 mm, five times worse. Stiffer is not always better; here softer springs (lower fn​) would help most.
